findings.title: Covert FTP Exfiltration Infrastructure

peirce_chain.firstness: Packed FTP server binary (smallftpd.exe, 191KB, VT 1/72 Packed.BDF.en) found at C:\Users\defaultprinter\smallftpd.exe. Configuration file ftpd.ini present with auto_run=1, port 21, user 'defaultprinter', password '12345'. Hidden user account 'defaultprinter' contains FTP, Dropbox, Telegram, WhatsApp shortcuts, security.evtx, NinaResearch.zip.
peirce_chain.secondness: FTP servers are not legitimate software on corporate research laptops. Binary packing evades AV detection (only Jiangmin detects). Account name 'defaultprinter' mimics Windows printer service — no legitimate IT deployment uses this naming pattern. auto_run=1 creates persistence without service registration. Password '12345' is deliberately trivial for retrieval convenience. DynDNS ensures external accessibility across IP changes. Entire C:\Users\PC User directory exposed — not a specific collaboration share. Habit incongruence: 10 anomalies detected, 99% compromise probability.
peirce_chain.thirdness: Deliberate construction of persistent, low-profile data exfiltration infrastructure. Carnegie authority-transfer technique: borrowing legitimacy from printer service naming to suppress analyst scrutiny. Multiple redundant exfiltration channels (FTP + Dropbox + Telegram + WhatsApp) indicate operational planning with backup pathways. security.evtx copied to user profile indicates counter-forensic awareness. This pattern requires tool knowledge, network configuration skills, and social engineering awareness that exceeds accidental misconfiguration.

findings.carnegie_pattern: Authority transfer via system service name masquerade (defaultprinter)
findings.devil_advocate: The FTP server could have been installed by IT for legitimate file sharing. The 'defaultprinter' account could be an automated IT provisioning artifact. REFUTATION: (1) No IT department installs packed binaries with trivial passwords. (2) DynDNS configuration has no benign explanation on a corporate laptop. (3) Exposing the entire home directory is inconsistent with controlled file sharing. (4) 10 habit anomalies confirmed by detect_habit_incongruence at 99% compromise probability. (5) security.evtx copy indicates counter-forensic monitoring. The benign hypothesis fails on all structural tests.
findings.corroboration: ART-003 (transfer log) confirms the FTP infrastructure was actively used for data exfiltration. ART-007 (registry) confirms user presence during transfer.

shannon_entropy.interpretation: Normal text range for artifact descriptions. Binary entropy not directly measurable from case file metadata.

findings.title: Confirmed IP Exfiltration of Level 5-8 Classified Material

peirce_chain.firstness: transfers.log records: '18/06/2016 18:21:49 Download started by defaultprinter [173.73.166.249] : c:\Users\defaultprinter\Desktop\temp.zip'. Download completed 18:21:50 (1 second). Five classified documents found on device: ZF DNA splice test notes.docx, Rapid cell regeneration research.docx, calculations on cell regroth.docx, zebrafish.pdf, Research to Weaponize the Ion Thruster.docx.
peirce_chain.secondness: IP 173.73.166.249 geolocates to Arlington, Virginia (Verizon FiOS residential, AS701) — in the Washington DC metropolitan area consistent with Stark Enterprises DC R&D location. 1-second transfer duration indicates pre-staged archive and brief, deliberate session. Same documents appeared on Chinese university research server 2016-06-22/23, exactly 4 days after transfer. Office temp files (~$) present, proving documents were actively opened. File named 'temp.zip' — deliberately generic to avoid scrutiny.
peirce_chain.thirdness: Complete exfiltration chain reconstructed: classified documents → pre-staged temp.zip → FTP download by co-conspirator at residential IP → 4-day cutout delay → Chinese university posting. The temporal gap suggests an intermediary transfer mechanism to obscure attribution. The deliberate genericness of 'temp.zip' and the 1-second retrieval window indicate a pre-arranged, rehearsed operation.

findings.devil_advocate: The transfer could have been legitimate file sharing with a colleague. The documents could be publicly available research. REFUTATION: (1) The documents are classified Level 5-8 Stark material — not public research. (2) The receiving IP is residential, not institutional. (3) The 4-day gap before Chinese university posting indicates deliberate staging, not coincidence. (4) temp.zip is a deliberately generic filename inconsistent with legitimate sharing. (5) The 1-second transfer window indicates pre-arrangement.
findings.corroboration: ART-007 (registry) confirms user was actively operating machine during transfer. ART-001/002 (FTP infrastructure) confirms the channel was purpose-built.

findings.title: User Active Presence During Exfiltration Window

peirce_chain.firstness: NTUSER.DAT registry timestamps: 21:55:03Z (Snipping Tool, Paint, Notepad, Sticky Notes), 21:59:55Z (Google Chrome), 22:22:13Z (File Explorer). FTP transfer at 22:21:49Z.
peirce_chain.secondness: Temporal correlation is exact: user activity spans 21:55-22:22Z, FTP transfer occurs at 22:21:49Z — 24 seconds before the last registry timestamp. Human jitter analysis confirms human operator (CV=1.023, variance=308934.22, std_dev=555.82). Human entropy analysis confirms probable human behavior (automation probability=0%). Snipping Tool at 21:55Z is consistent with capturing screenshots of classified research content for packaging.
peirce_chain.thirdness: User was physically present and actively operating the machine during the entire exfiltration window. This eliminates the hypothesis that the FTP server was triggered remotely without Vanko's knowledge. The activity pattern (Snipping Tool → Chrome → FTP transfer → File Explorer) is consistent with: prepare content → verify → execute transfer → confirm completion.

findings.devil_advocate: Vanko could have been using the machine for unrelated purposes while the FTP server ran autonomously in the background. REFUTATION: (1) The FTP server requires an incoming connection — someone at 173.73.166.249 deliberately initiated it. (2) Snipping Tool launch at 21:55Z is consistent with content preparation. (3) File Explorer at 22:22Z (24 seconds after transfer) is consistent with verification. The activity pattern maps precisely to the exfiltration operation.
findings.corroboration: ART-003 (transfer log) provides the exact timestamp. ART-005 (account profile) confirms the defaultprinter account context.

findings.title: Premeditated Wireless Reconnaissance Phase

peirce_chain.firstness: Two IEEE 802.11 monitor-mode packet captures: 'starbucks pcap.pcap' (685 packets, 155 seconds, 2016-03-04T17:25Z) and 'testpcap.pcap' (510 packets, 97 seconds, 2016-03-04T17:30Z). Radiotap headers confirm promiscuous wireless capture.
peirce_chain.secondness: Monitor-mode capture requires deliberate driver/hardware configuration — not default laptop behavior. Captures dated March 2016, three months before June 2016 exfiltration. SSIDs captured include Starbucks WiFi and other public networks. The presence of these captures on the same device used for exfiltration suggests operational awareness.
peirce_chain.thirdness: Wireless reconnaissance indicates advanced technical capability and an operational planning phase. However, this finding relies on a single source (pcap files) without direct temporal linkage to the exfiltration. The captures could relate to academic study (7-8-USB-Analysis.pptx also present on device). Rated SUSPICION per conservative Daubert standard.

findings.devil_advocate: The WiFi captures could be from a security class, CTF exercise, or academic research. The 7-8-USB-Analysis.pptx suggests Vanko had security training interests. PARTIAL ACCEPTANCE: This is plausible for the captures alone. However, the captures are on the same device used for exfiltration infrastructure, which weakens the benign interpretation. Downgraded to SUSPICION rather than INTENT due to single-source limitation.
findings.corroboration: Single source. No second artifact directly confirms reconnaissance purpose.
